messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Sita, a 31-year-old South Asian woman, has been a dedicated teacher for nearly ten years. She is married and deeply devoted to her profession, but in recent months, she has found herself increasingly haunted by an incident that occurred during one of her classes. While setting up a science experiment with her students, Sita accidentally spilled hot liquid on one of them, causing severe burns. Since the accident, Sita's world has been transformed into a series of triggers and vivid memories that feel as if they are happening in real time. The first major trigger is receiving praise or positive attention, which she finds confusing and disorienting. This confusion often leads her back to the memory of the incident, where she can still smell the acrid scent of burning fabric and the sterile odor of medical supplies from when paramedics arrived. One day, during a school staff meeting, Sita was praised for her innovative teaching methods. As colleagues congratulated her, she found herself overwhelmed by a sense of disorientation. The memory flashed before her eyes like a series of snapshots: her hands shaking as she held the beaker, the startled faces of the students, and the pained cries of the injured child. These images were so vivid that Sita felt as though she was reliving the moment. Sita's negative appraisals have deepened her sense of isolation and inadequacy. She has come to believe that she is no longer capable of performing the tasks that once defined her as a teacher. The self-blame she feels over the accident has made it difficult for her to look at herself or others without feeling like an outsider. This conviction has only intensified her memory intrusions, making them more persistent and vivid. Her negative appraisals have also heightened her sensitivity to triggers. Sita is particularly sensitive when discussions veer towards accidents or safety measures in the classroom. These conversations often lead her back to the scene of the incident, triggering intense memories that feel present rather than past. She finds herself avoiding such discussions at all costs, which has strained her relationships with colleagues who do not understand why she distances herself during these moments. Sita's avoidance behaviors have gradually seeped into other areas of her life as well. She has started to decline social invitations and professional events, feeling that any positive emotion might lead her back to the traumatic memory. This isolation has widened her sense of being an outsider, reinforcing her negative self-view. What finally brought Sita to seek help was a particularly distressing incident at work where she was asked to give a presentation on a new teaching technique. As she stood in front of her colleagues, preparing to speak, the smell of cleaning supplies from the room triggered a vivid flashback. She felt paralyzed and was unable to continue, which led to her feeling more self-blame and inadequacy. Sita is most afraid that this incident will define her forever, eroding any sense of confidence she once had as a teacher. At the same time, she is hopeful that with help, she might regain some control over her thoughts and memories, allowing her to reconnect with her students and colleagues without feeling trapped by her past actions.
